title: We played the flute (Matthew 11:1–19)
hookLine: too serious, too fun: why would Jesus repeat the insults about himself?
tomorrow: what do you do with a week that's simply too heavy?

cards: Post something goofy and the comments say: grow up. Post something serious and they say: so dramatic. Some people won't be pleased whichever way you go.
Jesus noticed the same thing. It starts with John the Baptist, in prison, sending a question: "Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?"

Jesus answers with what the messengers can see: the blind see, the lame walk, the poor hear good news. Then he turns to the crowd and does something odd. He repeats, out loud, the worst things people say about him.

teach.b: First he paints a playground: "It is like unto children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows, And saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented."

teach.h: A WEDDING TUNE, A FUNERAL SONG.
teach.b: A wedding, where someone pipes a tune and you dance. A funeral, where someone wails and you mourn. The other children won't play either one.

Then he names the two tunes, and here are the insults: "For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He hath a devil. The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners."
That's the puzzle solved. Set side by side, the two complaints cancel each other out. John fasted, and that was too much.
Jesus ate with tax collectors, and that was too much too. When someone has decided not to join, any tune will do as the excuse. Saying both insults aloud lets the crowd hear it.
Then one short line: "But wisdom is justified of her children." Wisdom is shown by what it grows. In Matthew, the fast and the feast are both invitations.

how: Some churches keep both kinds of seasons in their calendar, times of fasting and times of feasting, and some Christians read Matthew 11:16–19 as a reminder to keep both.

games.q: what does “we played the flute” mean?
o: an old wedding song sung at every feast
the music played in the temple courts
a game kids play: a tune nobody would dance to

games.q: the market game — tap the pairs.
p: they say, he hath a devil
the Son of man, eating and drinking
a friend of publicans and sinners

s: John the Baptist and Jesus lived the same way
John came neither eating nor drinking; the Son of man came eating and drinking.
Jesus was never accused of enjoying food and drink
they called him a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners.
in the picture, the children refuse both the dance and the mourning
we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented.

games.q: your team wins a big project the same morning a coworker learns her dad is sick. lunch is a party. what fits Jesus' picture?
o: party with the team; grief is private, so leave her be.
skip both, so you don't pick the wrong tune.
sit with her first, then go and celebrate with the team.
games.why: in the market, the children who refused both the dance and the mourning missed both. wisdom is justified of her children: there's a time for each tune.

practice: Bring back a song from someone else's good day: the one from their wedding, their graduation, the one they blast in the car. Let it play in your head while you breathe, and let yourself be glad for them, even a little.
If a sad song comes instead, someone's loss, stay with that one; it's an invitation too.

wordCard.voice: We played the flute. The children's complaint in the market, and Jesus' picture of a crowd that won't join in, whatever the tune.

orig.note: Greek: to play the flute or pipe. in Matthew 11:17 the children say, we piped unto you.

carryVoice: Your line: dance when they play. And when the song turns sad, mourn with them. Talk soon.
